newsitem.title: USA: BASEBALL-UMPIRES SUSPEND WALKOUT, ALOMAR APPEAL EXPEDITED.
newsitem.headline: BASEBALL-UMPIRES SUSPEND WALKOUT, ALOMAR APPEAL EXPEDITED.

text.p: Major League Baseball and its umpires reached an agreement minutes before post-season playoffs began Tuesday, averting a threatened walkout over the behaviour of Baltimore Orioles second baseman Roberto Alomar.

Baseball representatives agreed in a closed federal court session to expedite a hearing on Alomar's appeal of a five-game suspension for bumping and spitting at umpire John Hirschbeck, who ejected Alomar from a game Friday.
Umpires in turn agreed to call off their walkout and work through Thursday, the day of the expedited hearing before American League president Gene Budig.

The agreement was reached moments before the Orioles were to begin their afternoon playoff game against the Cleveland Indians at Camden Yards in Baltimore. The game started with regular umpires 14 minutes after its scheduled time of 1:05 p.m. EDT.
Replacement umpires had been waiting in the wings to officiate if needed.
"I see this as a significant victory for the umpires," Richard Phillips, attorney for the Major League Umpires Association, told reporters after the agreement was reached.
"They (baseball representatives) have conceded that they will conduct a hearing and render a decision on Thursday."

Said major league attorney Bill Schweitzer, "We came here today hopeful that we could get the umpires back on the field and we were successful through a compromise in being able to do that, so we're pleased about that."
Umpires had threatened to walk out until Alomar's suspension took effect. Under normal circumstances, the appeal would have delayed any penalty until the beginning of the 1997 season.
U.S. District Judge Edmund Ludwig did not rule on a request by the major leagues to order the umpires to work, and instead insisted the two sides find a way to reach agreement.
Under the agreement, if the appeal is heard and ruled on Thursday by the American League, the umpires are to work for the rest of the post-season.
A federal court hearing was scheduled for Friday at which the case would be revisited if either side felt the other acted in bad faith.

Phillips said in most cases player suspensions are upheld, and the umpires expect Alomar's to begin immediately if it is upheld. "The suspension should begin immediately. If it's not, we'll be back in here on Friday."
The umpires also will ask that the suspension be lengthened, he said.
Alomar was ejected by Hirschbeck Friday night in Toronto for arguing a called third strike. He bumped Hirschbeck and spat in the umpire's face before being restrained by manager Davey Johnson.
After the game, Alomar said he had "no regrets" about spitting on Hirschbeck and that the umpire had become "more bitter" since the death of his young son.
Alomar attempted Monday to short-circuit the ugliness surrounding the incident by issuing a release through the team that apologised to Hirschbeck and his family.
He also said he and the Orioles pledged $50,000 apiece for research of ALD, or adrenoleukodystrophy, a form of leukaemia that killed one of Hirschbeck's sons and now afflicts another.
"I wish to take this opportunity to apologise to John Hirschbeck and his family for any pain and embarrassment that my comments and actions may have caused them," Alomar said in Monday's statement.

"I deeply regret my disrespectful conduct towards a man that I know always gives his utmost as an umpire. Certainly, he has worked at least as hard as I have to make it to the majors. Notwithstanding what occurred, I have great respect for him and his profession."
